slides.title: Peripheral blood smear
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous or fingertip capillary blood; heel stick in babies

What it is used for: For a blood smear, blood is spread on a glass slide and treated with a special stain; a laboratory professional then checks the size, shape and number of red cells, white cells and platelets under a microscope. Automatic computer programs may be used to help.

A blood smear alone can't diagnose a disease, but with other tests it helps diagnose and monitor blood and bone marrow disorders, certain cancers of the blood, bone marrow and lymphatic system, infections and certain parasites.

slides.title: Peripheral blood smear
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: After an abnormal CBC, a smear confirms cell size and number and shows more about how the cells look, including their color. It is also ordered for symptoms of a blood-cell condition (fatigue, jaundice, unusual bleeding, easy bruising, fever, bone pain, swollen lymph nodes), to check treatment of anemia or blood cancer, and for flu-like symptoms in people living in or travelling to areas where malaria or babesiosis is common.

slides.title: Peripheral blood smear
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result
bullets: High: Results describe what the cells look like and how many there are, and anything else unusual, such as parasites. Abnormal red cells may be a sign of anemia, sickle cell disease, hemolytic anemia, thalassemia or bone marrow disorders; abnormal white cells of infection, leukemia or bone marrow disorders; abnormal platelets of thrombocytopenia, thrombocytosis or thrombocythemia.

slides.title: Peripheral blood smear
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed, though fasting may be required if other tests are ordered. Blood is drawn from a vein, sometimes by finger prick, and from the heel in babies.
Interferences: Severe illness, stress and blood transfusions can also cause abnormal smear results.
Limitations: Smear results alone usually can't diagnose a condition: the provider combines them with history, symptoms and other tests and may order more tests to find the cause.

slides.title: Malaria parasites (Plasmodium)
bullets: Members of the order Haemosporida live as parasites in the red blood cells — erythrocytes — of humans and warm-blooded animals; the most important member is the malaria plasmodium, which causes malaria in humans.

Four species mainly parasitise humans: Plasmodium vivax — tertian malaria (fever recurs every 48 hours); P. malariae — quartan malaria (every 72 hours); P. falciparum — tropical malaria (attacks every 24–48 hours, often very severe); P. ovale — tertian malaria (every 48 hours), very rare.
Plasmodium develops in two hosts: asexual multiplication and maturation of gametocytes occur in human red blood cells (first in liver cells), and sexual development in the Anopheles mosquito.
Unlike coccidia, the plasmodium’s life cycle runs only inside its hosts (mosquito and human) and does not leave into the external environment.

slides.title: Malaria parasites (Plasmodium)
bullets: Malaria is transmitted by a mosquito bite: sporozoites from the mosquito’s saliva enter human blood.

slides.title: Life cycle of the plasmodium (P. vivax as the example)
bullets: Sporozoites from the mosquito’s saliva enter human blood, reach liver and spleen tissue with the blood, and there feed and begin to multiply: the nucleus divides and merozoites form.

Merozoites enter red blood cells and grow at the expense of haemoglobin — this stage is called the trophozoite: at first, because of a vacuole in its centre, it looks like a ring, then the vacuole disappears and the parasite takes an amoeboid shape.
Trophozoites give rise to dividing schizonts; the schizont nucleus in the erythrocyte divides several times and 12–24 merozoites mature.

Merozoites rupture the erythrocyte and are released into the plasma (48 hours after the merozoite entered the cell) — this is exactly when a malaria attack begins; toxic substances such as melanin are released into the plasma together with the merozoites.

slides.title: Life cycle of the plasmodium (P. vivax as the example)
bullets: Merozoites enter healthy erythrocytes again and restart asexual development; after several rounds of schizogony, sexual forms — macro- and microgametocytes — appear in the blood.
Gametocytes develop further in the stomach of the Anopheles mosquito: gametes → zygote → ookinete → oocyst → thousands of sporozoites, which collect in the mosquito’s salivary gland.

slides.title: Blood changes in malaria
bullets: A patient with malaria develops marked anaemia: the erythrocyte count per 1 mm³ of blood can fall from the normal 5 million to 1 million (Dadayev).
The cause of the anaemia is destruction of erythrocytes when merozoites are released; toxic substances also enter the plasma.
Unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin rises when red-cell breakdown increases — in haemolytic anaemia, malaria, large haemorrhages into tissues and others (Yusupova et al., p. 143).
Malaria is also listed among the causes of neutropenia (a fall in neutrophils) (p. 40).
Monocytosis occurs in protozoal infections — malaria, leishmaniasis (p. 44); monocytes can phagocytose malaria plasmodia (p. 57).

rows: negative smears every 12–24 hours, 3 series in total series

slides.title: Why order a blood smear for flu-like symptoms after travel to a malaria area?
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: for example malaria or babesiosis parasites.

Basis: Parasites may be seen on the smear under the microscope.

slides.title: Epidemiology, etiopathogenesis of malaria?
bullets: 1. Causative agents: Plasmodium falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae, P. knowlesi; vector – the female Anopheles mosquito.
2. Life cycle: sporozoites – liver stage (hypnozoites in P. vivax/ovale – relapses), then the erythrocytic cycle and gametocytes.
3. Pathogenesis: destruction of erythrocytes – fever attacks and anemia; in P. falciparum cytoadherence – severe malaria (brain, kidney).
4. Epidemiology: tropical regions, imported cases; transfusion and vertical transmission are rare.
5. When suspected (travel history + fever) – urgent laboratory testing.

slides.title: Laboratory diagnosis of malaria?
bullets: 1. Microscopy is the main method: thick smear (finding the parasite, sensitivity) and thin smear (species identification); Giemsa staining.

2. Calculating parasitemia (WHO MM-SOP-09): in a thick smear parasites/µL = parasites counted × 8000 / leukocytes counted (if the actual leukocyte count is unavailable, 8000/µL is assumed); if there are ≥100 parasites per field, the proportion (%) of infected erythrocytes is calculated on the thin smear.
3. If negative, repeat smears at 12–24 hour intervals (3 series in total).
4. Rapid tests (RDT, antigens) – where microscopy is not available; confirm the result by microscopy and quantify.
5. PCR – for species identification and low parasitemia; serology is not for acute diagnosis.
6. Quality: qualification of microscopists, standard stain pH, external quality assessment.

slides.title: Epidemiology, etiopathogenesis, laboratory diagnosis of malaria?
bullets: 1. Causative agents and vector: five Plasmodium species, the Anopheles mosquito; life cycle – liver and erythrocytic stages.
2. Pathogenesis: destruction of erythrocytes (fever, anemia), severe complications in P. falciparum.
3. Microscopy: thick and thin smear, Giemsa; thick – detection, thin – species.
4. Calculating parasitemia (WHO MM-SOP-09): in the thick smear assuming 8000 leukocytes/µL (if no actual WBC), at high parasitemia the percentage of infected erythrocytes on the thin smear.
5. RDT, PCR (species and low parasitemia), if negative repeat after 12–24 hours; serology is not for acute diagnosis.
